title: Warding Off Classroom AI
author: Peter Greene
summary: Greene argues that the entire apparatus of AI-proofing classrooms — detector bots, chatbot bans, anti-cheating policies — is the wrong response, both because it does not work and because it misdiagnoses the problem. Detection tools falsely accuse students, and forbidding AI is as futile as banning Cliff Notes or Wikipedia was. He locates cheating in three durable causes: students believing success will be too hard or time-consuming, believing the stakes of failure are too high, and lacking any sense of the actual point of their education. His central claim is that 'AI most easily rushes into places where humanity has already been hollowed out,' and that modern test-centric, outcome-based ed reform has pushed classrooms toward being product-centered rather than human-centered — exactly the conditions under which a machine can out-produce students. Citing Boston College professor Carlo Rotella's New York Times case for more humanity in the humanities, Greene recommends process-focused writing instruction, in-class work, and oral and pen-and-paper assessment. The remedy he lands on is not preventative rules but building a classroom so thoroughly human in its context, values, and purpose that AI must either serve that purpose or be left out.
points: Greene rejects AI detection and bans on both practical and pedagogical grounds: detector bots are unreliable and unfairly accuse students, and prohibition is as ineffective as banning Cliff Notes or Wikipedia ever was.

He roots cheating in three enduring conditions — believing the work is too hard or time-consuming, believing the stakes of failure are too high, and lacking any felt sense of the point of education — which technology fixes cannot touch.

The load-bearing insight is that 'AI most easily rushes into places where humanity has already been hollowed out,' so a product-centered classroom created by test-driven reform is uniquely vulnerable because a machine can generate the artifacts faster than students.

Drawing on Carlo Rotella, Greene endorses concrete AI-resistant practices — pen-and-paper and oral testing, teaching the process of writing rather than just assigning papers, and shifting weight to what happens in the classroom.

His alternative to rules is purpose: a teacher who knows their foundational 'why' can judge any AI tool by whether it serves the goal of helping young humans grow into their humanity, rather than adopting tech ass-backwards and retrofitting a use for it.
quotes: Simply forbidding it is as effective as was the banning of Cliff Notes or Wikipedia.
Trying to chase the chatbots away is simply not going to work. More than that, it is not going to help students grasp an education.
As I’ve now said many times, AI most easily rushes into places where humanity has already been hollowed out.

Modern ed reform, with its test-centric data-driven outcome-based approach has pushed us even further toward classrooms that are product-centered rather than human-centered. But if class is all about the product, then AI can produce those artifacts far faster and more easily than human students.
The key to an AI-resistant classroom is not a batch of preventative rules.
Planning the details of a unit is hard--but it gets much easier if you know why you are teaching the unit in the first place.
